## Description

The false position, or regula falsi, method solves a single equation $f(x) = 0$ for a real root inside an interval $[a, b]$ on which $f$ changes sign.
Starting from $[a_1, b_1] = [a, b]$, it keeps a sign-change bracket $[a_n, b_n]$ at every step and takes as the new point the x-intercept of the secant line through $(a_n, f(a_n))$ and $(b_n, f(b_n))$:

$$
c_n = \frac{a_n f(b_n) - b_n f(a_n)}{f(b_n) - f(a_n)}.
$$

If $f(a_n)$ and $f(c_n)$ have opposite signs, the next bracket is $[a_n, c_n]$; otherwise it is $[c_n, b_n]$.
Unlike bisection (which uses the midpoint), Regula Falsi weights the new point toward whichever endpoint has a smaller $|f|$ value, often giving faster convergence — but one endpoint can remain fixed for many iterations.

The method needs only that $f$ be continuous on $[a, b]$ with $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ of opposite signs.
Mathews' Regula Falsi theorem then guarantees that the points $c_n$ converge to a zero $x^*$ of $f$ in $[a, b]$.
If $[a, b]$ contains several zeros, the method finds one of them, and a sign change across a discontinuity need not enclose a zero at all.

The guarantee says nothing about speed.
In general, if $f''$ is positive throughout $[a, b]$ or negative throughout, so that $f$ is convex or concave there, the same endpoint stays in the bracket at every step and the convergence is only linear.
With $b$ as that fixed endpoint and $e_n = c_n - x^*$,

$$
e_{n+1} \approx C\, e_n, \qquad C = 1 - \frac{f'(x^*)\,(b - x^*)}{f(b)}, \qquad 0 < C < 1,
$$

for large $n$ (with $a$ in place of $b$ when $a$ is the endpoint that stays).
Both animations have $f$ convex and $b$ fixed.
In [Case A](#case-a), the error ratios $e_{n+1}/e_n$ of the computed iterates settle at $0.2513$, and in [Case B](#case-b) at $0.0501$, matching $C$ and beating the factor $1/2$ of bisection.

Two consequences can mislead.
Because one endpoint never moves, the bracket width $b_n - a_n$ does not go to zero: in Case A it stays above $2 - x^* \approx 0.6348$, so a stopping test must use $|c_n - c_{n-1}|$ or $|f(c_n)|$, not the width.
And when $f$ is strongly curved, $C$ is close to 1: for $f(x) = x^{10} - 1$ on $[0, 1.3]$, $C \approx 0.765$, and regula falsi needs 61 steps to bring $|c_n - 1|$ below $10^{-6}$, where bisection needs 20.

[Bisection](../bisection-method/) keeps the same kind of bracket but always halves it, the [Secant Method](../secant-method/) applies the same formula to the two most recent iterates without keeping a sign change, converging faster at a simple root (order about $1.618$) but without the guarantee, [Newton-Raphson](../newton-raphson-method/) uses the tangent line instead of a secant, and [Brent's Method](../brents-method/) combines a bracket with interpolation steps and falls back on bisection.

## Animations

Each animation below shows the **secant diagram** for Regula Falsi. At each step, a secant line is drawn through the two bracket endpoints $(a, f(a))$ and $(b, f(b))$; its x-intercept $c$ becomes the new estimate. In each frame after the first, the dashed secant passes through the endpoints of the previous bracket, while the shaded band shows the updated bracket, which has the new point $c$ (red) as one endpoint.

Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

### Case A — Convergent, $f(x) = x^3 + 4x^2 - 10$, $[a, b] = [-1, 2]$ {#case-a}

**Behavior:** The method converges to the real root $x^* \approx 1.3652$. The right endpoint $b = 2$ stays fixed throughout: $f(-1) < 0$ and every false-position point $c$ also satisfies $f(c) < 0$ ($f$ is convex on the bracket), so the algorithm keeps replacing $a$ with $c$ ($a = -1, 0, 0.8333, 1.2088, \dots$) while $b = 2$ holds. This "one-sided" stagnation is characteristic of Regula Falsi and distinguishes it from the symmetric bracketing of bisection.

[Julia source](regulafalsiaa.jl)

![Regula Falsi animation for f(x)=x³+4x²−10 on [−1,2]: the secant line from bracket endpoints walks toward the root near x=1.37, with the right endpoint fixed and successive false-position points converging from the left.](regulafalsiaa.gif)

### Case B — Convergent (one-sided), $f(x) = x - \cos(x)$, $[a, b] = [0, 1]$ {#case-b}

**Behavior:** The method converges to the "Dottie number" $x^* \approx 0.7391$, the unique fixed point of cosine. The right endpoint $b = 1$ (where $f(1) \approx 0.4597$) remains fixed throughout, because $f$ is convex on $[0, 1]$ and every false-position point satisfies $f(c) < 0$; the points advance from the left ($c = 0.6851, 0.7363, 0.7389, \dots$). This is a clean illustration of one-sided convergence: the bracket shrinks only on the left side, yet the secant intercept homes in on the root accurately.

[Julia source](regulafalsibb.jl)

![Regula Falsi animation for f(x)=x−cos(x) on [0,1]: the secant from bracket endpoints converges to the Dottie number x*≈0.739, with the right endpoint fixed at 1 while the left endpoint steps in.](regulafalsibb.gif)
